chunks: [Those who are ignorant (or subject to doubt):]

The third man is he who heard the Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) ordering something, and later He forbade it, but he did not know it; or he heard Him forbidding something, and later He ordered it, but he did not know it. Thus, he retained in his memory what had been abrogated, and did not retain the abrogating [ruling]. If he knew that it was abrogated, he would reject it; and if the Muslims knew, when they heard it from him, that it was abrogated, they would reject it.
ai.seo_question: What characterizes a narrator who is subject to doubt due to ignorance of abrogation in hadith sciences?
ai.summary: Sharif al-Radi identifies this specific category of 'ahl al-shubha' (people of doubt) as a narrator who memorizes the abrogated (mansukh) ruling while missing the abrogating (nasikh) one, or vice versa, due to a lack of awareness regarding the chronological sequence of revelation. This highlights a critical nuance in Shia hadith criticism where the validity of a narration depends not just on the narrator's memory, but on their understanding of the temporal context of the Prophet's commands. The text implies that such errors are excusable if the community also lacked knowledge of the abrogation, underscoring the communal role in preserving the integrity of the Sunnah.
